title: Kisa Gotami's child
hook: a young mother carries her dead son from house to house, asking for medicine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monk who was stoned: Angulimala blessed a birth and bore the town's anger. Your line was born into a new life. Who did you wish ease on? Day seventy-four.

This one is gentle, and it's sad, so go easy on yourself as you listen. If you've lost someone, you already know the part of grief where you can't accept it yet. Where you keep their phone number. Where you set the table for one too many. Where you think, surely, there's something that can still be done. A young woman named Kisa Gotami is standing in the street of a city, holding a small boy on her hip. He's her only child. He's just learned to walk. And he has died. She won't put him down. She's going from door to door, asking every person she meets for medicine.
screen: `GO EASY ON YOURSELF.` → `WHEN YOU CAN'T ACCEPT IT YET.` → `A MOTHER, GOING DOOR TO DOOR.`

segments.voice: Her story is told in the commentaries, the explanations written down alongside the old texts, and her own poems survive among the verses of the elder nuns. Her name is part of the story. Kisa means thin. She was Gotami, of the Gotama clan, the thin one, born into a poor family. She married into a wealthy house, and the story says her husband's family looked down on her. Then she had a son, and everything changed. She was honored now. She belonged. The child was her place in the world as much as her joy. And then he died, very young. So she lifts him onto her hip and walks. Can you give me medicine for my son? And people stare. Some laugh at her. Some turn away. Who has ever heard of medicine for the dead? She keeps walking. She carries him everywhere. What's striking is that the story doesn't call her foolish. It doesn't rush her. It lets her walk, and it lets her be refused, house after house, because this is what grief does. The mind can't take in the loss all at once, so it goes looking for a way around it. Finally someone sees her differently. A wise man, the story says, understands that she's out of her mind with grief, and doesn't mock her. He tells her: I don't have medicine. But I know someone who might. Go to the Buddha. So she carries her son to where the Buddha is teaching, and stands at the edge of the crowd, and asks him. Do you know a medicine for my child? We'll stop there for today, with her question. Tomorrow, his answer.
screen: `KISA MEANS THIN.` · `THE CHILD WAS HER PLACE.` · `MEDICINE FOR THE DEAD?` · `GO TO THE BUDDHA.` · then, large: `SHE CARRIED HIM EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit quietly with someone's grief. Settle and breathe. Think of someone you know who is grieving, recently or long ago. Maybe it's you. You don't have to fix anything. You don't have to find the right words. Just picture sitting beside them, the way a friend sits at a hospital bed. Let your breath be slow and steady, as if you were breathing for both of you. Stay. That's all. The bell holds the time.
Kisa Gotami's child. A young mother, the thin Gotami, carrying her dead son from door to door, asking for medicine.
Your line: she carried him everywhere. Today, if someone you know is carrying a loss, don't try to fix it. Just ask about the one they lost. Day seventy-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across traditions tell Kisa Gotami's story at funerals and in times of grief, and her own verses are preserved in the Therigatha, the poems of the elder nuns.
